guidance:
Use only the content of Table 1 to define structure and values. Do not invent columns, rows, or numbers, and do not treat narrative text as data.

1) Table title and scope
- Take `table_title` directly from the caption of Table 1.
- Ignore all other tables and figures. If text or footnotes help you understand layout, use them only for interpretation, not as a source of values.

2) Columns and headers
- Reconstruct the header from left to right before creating any cells.
- Add every explicit data column header to `columns` (groups, arms, timepoints, statistics such as effect size, etc.).
- When headers are stacked or multi-level, treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Form each `column_label` by combining higher-level and leaf text (e.g., "Group: Statistic").
- The leftmost label column may have its own heading. If it exists, include that heading in `columns`, but never create data cells for that column; its entries become `row_label` and sometimes `row_group`.
- Do not invent aggregate or "Total" columns unless they are explicitly printed as headers.
- Every `column_label` used in cells must appear exactly once in `columns`; do not create duplicate or slightly varied names for the same column.

3) Row_group vs. row_label
- Read down the first column and separate structure from data:
  • Section / category headings: visually distinct, spanning columns or followed by several related rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with values in data columns.
- Use the text of each section heading as `row_group` for all subsequent data rows it clearly governs.
- For each data row under a section, set `row_group` to that section heading and `row_label` to the specific item name on that row.
- Rows that are not under any clear heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has values on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is the broader category; `row_label` is the individual row item. Never place a category name in `row_label` while using an item name as `row_group`.
- When the same section or item appears in multiple places, reuse its text exactly so grouping remains consistent.

4) Creating cells and capturing values
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible value (numbers, percentages, text, symbols) in the body of Table 1, create exactly one cell object with fields: `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, `value`.
- Copy `value` verbatim, preserving punctuation, spaces, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers such as "N/A" or dashes when they appear as values.
- A printed zero is a real value and must be included.
- Do not create cells for blank entries. Do not infer, calculate, or move values between rows or columns.

5) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work row by row: for each data row, scan across all data columns and ensure every non-empty table entry produces exactly one cell.
- Do not create cells for pure header or section lines that have no data values.
- Do not add values that appear only in notes or narrative unless they are clearly placed in a specific row/column cell in the table.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique; never emit more than one cell for the same position.

6) String consistency
- Use table wording verbatim for `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, capitalization, spacing, and symbols.
- Check that every `column_label` used in `cells` matches exactly one entry in `columns` and that category headings used as `row_group` are identical across their rows.

Apply these rules to any Table 1 layout, focusing on correctly identifying sections, rows, and headers so every non-empty table value is captured once in the right position.
